prompt: Why didn't Harvard have calculus classes when it first opened?
answer:
Harvard could not offer calculus when it opened in 1636 because **calculus had not yet been developed as a formal mathematical subject**. Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed their versions independently in the 1660s and published major work in the 1680s.

Harvard did teach mathematics from about 1638—especially arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy—but its early curriculum emphasized Latin, Greek, theology, rhetoric, logic, and classical philosophy. Calculus was added much later, becoming established at Harvard in the eighteenth century, particularly under Professor John Winthrop.

So the claim is broadly true, though “calculus was invented” oversimplifies the fact that it grew out of earlier mathematical work.
